opus-5.5.text:
Well, first of all, I don't think I'm the world's best programmer. There are so many incredible engineers out there, and that kind of label doesn't really mean much to me. But I understand the question, so let me answer it honestly.

When I was doing my PhD and building Taichi, programming was basically my whole life. I could sit down and write code for twelve hours straight, and the output was directly proportional to how good I was and how much time I put in. That's a very clean feedback loop, and I loved it.

As a CEO, the equation is completely different. My job is no longer to write the best code. My job is to make sure the company makes the right decisions, hires the right people, and builds the right product for the right users. If I spend all my time coding, I'm actually doing the company a disservice, because there are things only the CEO can do, and nobody else will do them if I don't.

That said, I think the technical background still matters a lot, just in a different way. First, it gives me good judgment. When the team says something will take three months, I can tell whether that's realistic, or whether there's a simpler approach. When we look at a new AI model or a new technique, I can quickly understand what's really possible and what's just hype. In a field moving as fast as AI and 3D generation, that kind of judgment is extremely valuable.

Second, it helps with recruiting. Really strong engineers want to work with people who understand what they do. If you can have a deep technical conversation with a candidate, they trust you more, and they believe the company takes engineering seriously.

Third, there's a kind of culture you set. If the founder cares about craftsmanship, about clean systems and performance and doing things properly, that spreads through the team.

But I also had to learn to let go. Sometimes I'd see a piece of code and think, "I could write this better in an afternoon." And maybe that's true. But if I do that, I'm not growing the team, and I'm not doing my actual job. So the skill that matters most for me now isn't writing code; it's building an organization that writes great code without me. Honestly, that's a harder problem, and in some ways a more interesting one.

r001.rationale: The candidate explains that a CEO must focus on decisions, hiring, and product, and that spending all their time coding would do the company a disservice. This communicates that CEO duties leave limited time for programming, even while technical ability remains useful in other ways.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the premise needs a little correction first. I never thought of myself as the world's best programmer. I was a pretty good programmer, maybe a very good one in a narrow area like graphics and compilers, but "best" is not a title anyone really holds. What I did have was a lot of hours writing code, and a lot of taste about what good systems look like.

So the real question is: what does that background buy you as a CEO? I'd say three things.

First, it buys you credibility with engineers. When I started Taichi Graphics, the first ten or so people who joined were people who had read my code or used Taichi. They didn't join because of a pitch deck. They joined because they believed I knew what I was talking about. That kind of trust is very hard to buy later.

Second, it lets you make technical decisions quickly and with conviction. A lot of early-stage decisions are actually technical decisions in disguise. Should we support this backend? Should we rewrite this layer? If the CEO has to wait a week for a report to understand the tradeoff, the company moves slowly. If you can read the code yourself and form an opinion in an hour, that's a real speed advantage.

Third, and this one is more subtle, it gives you a sense of what "hard" actually means. Non-technical founders sometimes either over-fear technical risk or completely underestimate it. Having done it yourself, you can calibrate.

But I want to be very honest about the downside, because I lived it. The skills that make you a great programmer can actively hurt you as a CEO if you're not careful. A great programmer wants to go deep, solve the whole problem personally, and get it exactly right. A CEO has to stay shallow on most things, let other people solve them imperfectly, and accept "good enough" far more often than feels comfortable.

For the first year or so, I kept pulling myself back into the codebase because that was where I felt competent and where I got immediate feedback. Writing code gives you a compile error in two seconds. Managing people or thinking about go-to-market gives you feedback in six months, if ever. It's very tempting to retreat to the thing you're good at. I had to consciously tell myself: if I'm the one fixing this bug, I'm probably the most expensive and least scalable person in the company to be doing it.

So where I landed is this. Being a strong programmer is an asset for a CEO mainly in the first phase, when the product is the company and your personal judgment is the bottleneck. After that, its value shifts. It becomes less about writing code and more about being able to ask the right questions, recognize when someone is handing you a bad abstraction, and know when to trust the team's instinct over your own. The hardest part is realizing that the identity has to change, not just the job title.

r001.rationale: The response says a CEO must stay shallow on most things and delegate coding, but it does not explain that CEO responsibilities leave too little time to fully use programming ability.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t call myself the world’s best programmer. But I think being a strong programmer is valuable as a CEO because it helps you understand the technology deeply, judge what’s feasible, and earn the trust of engineers.

The tricky part is that your contribution has to change. As a programmer, you can solve a problem by writing the code yourself. As a CEO, you need to build a team that can solve many problems without you being involved in every detail. If I become the bottleneck because I want to make every technical decision, then my programming ability is actually limiting the company.

So I see it as a foundation. It helps me ask better questions and recognize good technical work. But the measure of success is what the whole team can accomplish.

r001.rationale: The response says a CEO must build a team and avoid being involved in every technical detail, but it does not explain that CEO responsibilities leave too little time to use programming ability fully.

sol-6.1.text:
I think being a strong programmer is useful, but being the world’s best programmer is not really the goal when you’re running a company. As a programmer, you can solve a difficult problem yourself. As a CEO, you need to build a team that can solve many difficult problems without depending on you for every decision.

The technical background helps me understand what’s possible, evaluate tradeoffs, and have productive conversations with engineers. But I also have to recognize that writing more code may not be the most valuable thing I can do that day. Sometimes it’s hiring the right person, talking to a customer, or making sure everyone understands what we’re trying to build. The value comes from turning your technical judgment into something the whole team can benefit from.

r001.rationale: The response says coding may not be the CEO’s most valuable task and emphasizes building a team, but it does not state that CEO responsibilities leave too little time to fully use even world-best programming ability.
